title: "Guts Enough Not to Fight Back"
text:
In 1945 no black player had appeared in major league baseball for more than sixty years. Branch Rickey, president of the Brooklyn Dodgers, set out to change that, and he chose Jackie Robinson, a former UCLA star and Army officer then playing in the Negro Leagues.

On August 28, 1945, Rickey met Robinson in his Brooklyn office. According to both men's later accounts, Rickey spent hours acting out what Robinson would face: insults from opposing players, racist taunts from crowds, hotel clerks refusing him rooms, umpires against him, pitchers throwing at his head. Robinson, who had been court-martialed and acquitted in the Army for refusing to move to the back of a bus, asked if Rickey was looking for a player who was afraid to fight back. Rickey answered, in the words Robinson later recorded, that he was looking for a ballplayer with guts enough not to fight back.

Robinson agreed to absorb the abuse without retaliating, at least at first. He played for Montreal in 1946 and joined the Dodgers on April 15, 1947. He endured everything Rickey had predicted, and more. He was named Rookie of the Year in 1947 and the league's Most Valuable Player in 1949. After his first years he spoke out freely.
lesson: Restraint under provocation, chosen for a larger goal, is a form of strength. Sometimes the hardest thing a leader does is not react.
source: Jackie Robinson, I Never Had It Made (1972); Branch Rickey's accounts
